title: Analyst Forecasting Ability and the Stock Price Reaction to Forecast Revisions

models.model_label: Forecast revision response by analyst ability group (80% threshold)
models.sample_description: Individual analyst forecast revision events for one-year-ahead annual earnings announced in 1990–1994. The data intersect Compustat, CRSP and I/B/E/S; events require the relevant earnings, three-day return-window, prior analyst-firm forecast-ability and forecast-surprise data. Firms must have at least five brokerage houses following them in each year 1988–1994, and each analyst-firm pair must have at least five forecasts in the preceding two years with at least one in each year. The three-day revision window must not overlap another same-firm revision, earnings announcement or dividend declaration. The final sample has 15,446 revision events.
models.method_details: The source presents a regression equation and coefficient t-statistics, but does not identify OLS or another underlying estimator; no estimator is inferred from the linear form.
models.equation_text: R_ijt = β_0 + β_1(FR_ijt × SUP_ijt) + β_2(FR_ijt × NOR_ijt) + β_3(FR_ijt × INF_ijt).

standard_errors.details: Table 4 reports coefficient t-statistics and F-tests with p-values for pairwise differences in the FR response coefficients. It does not specify a standard-error correction or clustering method.

estimation_procedure.description: Full-sample Table 4 regression compares forecast-surprise slopes across superior, normal, and inferior analyst categories through FR-by-category interactions. The 80% classification threshold is retained as the selected measure; 90% and 70% thresholds are reported as sensitivity checks, and the later spillover and announcement-timing analyses are not part of this principal model.

independent_variables.name: FR_ijt × SUP_ijt
independent_variables.definition: Forecast surprise multiplied by SUP_ijt, which is one if analyst j is classified as superior for firm i at time t and zero otherwise. Forecast surprise is the analyst’s current EPS forecast less the same analyst’s most recent EPS forecast for the same firm, divided by firm i’s share price two days before the revision. At the selected 80% threshold, superior means 80% or more of that analyst’s forecasts for the firm in the preceding two years were closer to actual earnings than the contemporaneous I/B/E/S consensus. Table 4 also places equality at 80% in the normal range, so assignment at that boundary is unresolved.

sample_extraction.data_section_full_text:
2. Sample and Data

The sample is chosen from the intersection of firms contained in the COMPUSTAT Industrial, Full Coverage, and Research files, the CRSP Daily File, and the I/B/E/S Detail History
file for 1988 to 1994. Only forecast revisions announced in the years 1990 through 1994 are
used in the tests. Data from 1988 and 1989 are used to generate analyst forecasting ability
measures for the year 1990; 1989 and 1990 data are used to develop the 1991 forecasting
ability measures, and so forth. To avoid cluttering the analysis, we restrict our attention
to one-year-ahead forecasts of annual earnings. Also, for ease in aggregating the data, we
exclude firms that make a change in fiscal year-end during the seven-year sample period. A
forecast revision is included in the sample if there exist (a) COMPUSTAT data for annual
earnings per share before extraordinary items and discontinued operations for the earnings
being forecast, (b) daily stock price and returns data from CRSP for the three-day interval
centered on the revision date <sup>1</sup>, (c) sufficient I/B/E/S data to develop an analyst forecasting
ability measure from prior forecasts by the same analyst for the same firm, and (d) I/B/E/S

market earnings expectation.

The most restrictive data availability condition is the one imposed in order to develop
a measure of analyst forecasting ability. For the empirical forecasting ability measure
to reliably distinguish between analysts with high and low forecasting ability, the focus
must be on firms that are followed by several analysts continuously over a period of years.
Accordingly, the sample includes a forecast revision only if the firm for which the earnings
are being forecast is followed by at least five brokerage houses in each year for the entire

sample period, 1988 through 1994. In addition, a forecast revision by a particular analyst is
included in the sample only if that analyst has made five forecasts of the earnings of the same
firm in the preceding two years, with at least one forecast in each year. These conditions
cause the sample to be composed of forecasts of earnings of large, widely followed firms.
For example, 82% of the forecast revisions included in the sample are for the earnings of
firms listed on the New York Stock Exchange. The restrictive nature of the sample suggests
caution in extrapolating the research results to firms not widely followed by analysts.

One additional set of constraints is placed on the sample: a forecast revision is included
in the sample only if the three-day event window around the revision announcement date,

[−1 , 0 , +1], does not overlap the event window for a potentially confounding event. Operationally, a forecast revision is dropped from the sample if its three-day event window
overlaps the three-day event window for any other forecast revision announcement for the
same firm, or if it overlaps the five-day event window centered on an earnings announcement
or dividend declaration date for the firm. This restriction is an attempt to isolate, as much
as possible, the price reaction to individual forecast revisions. These restrictions are similar
to those imposed by Waymire (1984) in an attempt to mitigate the potentially confounding
effects on tests of announcement period reactions to management earnings forecasts. The
final sample contains 15,446 observations
